transcript.text: My Panasonic NN-ST45KWBPQ is sparking inside when I heat soup, little blue flashes on the right-hand wall and a crackling noise. I stopped it. Is it safe?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Stop using the microwave now: switch it off at the socket and unplug it, and don't run it again (not even empty) until we know why it sparked. Never take the outer casing off — parts inside can hold a lethal charge even when it is unplugged. No, it is not safe to use. Please unplug the microwave immediately and do not run it again until a qualified engineer has inspected it. The blue flashes on the right-hand wall are almost probably caused by arcing at the waveguide cover (the small rectangular panel on the side wall). This happens when food splatter burns onto the cover or if the material itself is damaged. Because this involves high-voltage components and requires dismantling, you should not attempt to fix it yourself. If you are comfortable doing so with the appliance unplugged, you can check the waveguide cover for obvious holes or severe charring, but do not use the microwave even if it looks okay, as internal damage may not be visible. Please arrange for an engineer to visit.

I've unplugged it. There's a cardboard-like panel on the right wall with a black burnt spot and greasy splatter on it, and I saw a wisp of smoke from that spot once before it stopped when I turned it off. Is that panel something I can replace myself rather than calling an engineer?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. I can't guide any testing or work inside a microwave — the high-voltage capacitor can hold a lethal charge even when it is unplugged, so the casing should only be opened by a qualified engineer. No, you should not replace that panel yourself. That 'cardboard-like' panel is the waveguide cover (usually mica), which protects the internal electronics from food splatter while letting microwaves through. Because it has burnt and smoked, the high-voltage component behind it may also be damaged, and accessing it requires dismantling the microwave casing—something that is extremely dangerous due to lethal voltages even when unplugged. Please contact Panasonic support or a qualified appliance engineer to inspect and repair this safely.
